claim: Sox2 and Oct4 work in concert to specify the earliest lineages in the mammalian embryo.
source: The transcription factors (TFs) Sox2 and Oct4 work in concert to specify the earliest lineages in the mammalian embryo (Pesce and Schöler, 2001; Avilion et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Pesce and Schöler, 2001; Avilion et al., 2003)

claim: Chen et al. previously undertook an extensive single-molecule analysis of the dynamics of Sox2 and Oct4 in living cells.
source: Chen et al. previously undertook an extensive single-molecule analysis of the dynamics of Sox2 and Oct4 in living cells to determine how these TFs found their cognate sites on DNA (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2014

claim: Eukaryotic genomes contain multiple energy-expending mechanisms that reorganise chromatin, remodel nucleosomes and post-translationally modify regulators.
source: One of the most striking differences between eukaryotic genomes and eubacterial ones is the presence of multiple energy-expending mechanisms, which reorganise chromatin, remodel nucleosomes and post-translationally modify regulators.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about eukaryotic genome regulation

claim: There is debate about whether pioneer TFs like Sox2 and Oct4 can open chromatin without external energy sources.
source: There is debate, for instance, as to whether pioneer TFs, like Sox2 and Oct4, can open chromatin without relying on external sources of energy (Cirillo et al., 2002; Iwafuchi-Doi and Zaret, 2016) or whether they recruit ATP-dependent chromatin remodellers to undertake this (Voss et al., 2011; Swinstead et al., 2016; Zaret et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies presenting different views

claim: Kinetic proofreading is an energy-expending mechanism that can reduce error rates below the thermodynamic limit.
source: This limit is much higher than the very low error rates observed in practice and Hopfield introduced kinetic proofreading as an energy-expending mechanism which could account for this enhanced functionality.
evidence: Supported by reference to Hopfield's work

claim: Energy expenditure may be implicated in the sharp response of early developmental genes.
source: More recently, we have identified the analogous 'Hopfield barrier' for sharpness in gene regulation and suggested that energy expenditure may be implicated in the sharp response of early developmental genes (Estrada et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to authors' prior work

claim: Chen et al.'s single-molecule data suggest that TFs move between specifically bound and not specifically bound states.
source: These data suggest that the TF moves back and forth between two distinct states, one in which it is specifically bound to sites on DNA and one in which it is not specifically bound.
evidence: Based on interpretation of Chen et al.'s single-molecule measurements

claim: Chen et al. assumed that TF binding rates to DNA equal the rates at which TFs move from not specifically bound to specifically bound states.
source: For the second, they assumed that the rates at which the TF moved from being specifically bound to not being specifically bound, and vice versa, as determined from their single-molecule data, were 'good estimates' for the rates at which the TF unbound from, and bound to, DNA, respectively, (Chen et al., 2014, page S7).
evidence: Describes an assumption made by Chen et al.

claim: Chen et al.'s assumption about binding rates is correct for unbinding but not for binding.
source: This is correct for the unbinding rate but, as we will explain in more detail below, it is not correct for the binding rate.
evidence: Based on biophysical analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: Chen et al. used two cell lines in which one TF was fluorescently labeled and the other was inducibly expressed.
source: They therefore used two cell lines, in each of which one of the TFs was fluorescently labeled and measured while the other TF was inducibly expressed.
evidence: Describes the experimental design of Chen et al.

claim: Chen et al. assumed that when the second TF was inducibly expressed its binding sites were saturated.
source: Second, Chen et al. assumed that when the second TF was inducibly expressed its binding sites were saturated. This was an oversimplification.
evidence: Describes and critiques an assumption made by Chen et al.

claim: Sox2 and Oct4 exhibit negative reciprocity according to Chen et al.'s data.
source: The data acquired by Chen et al. show that Sox2 and Oct4 exhibit negative reciprocity, which means, in this case, that the fractional binding of Sox2 (ie: the proportion of Sox2-binding sites occupied by Sox2) decreases when Oct4 is induced but the fractional binding of Oct4 increases when Sox2 is induced.
evidence: Based on analysis of Chen et al.'s data using the reciprocity concept

claim: The single-locus model cannot exhibit negative reciprocity at thermodynamic equilibrium.
source: We find that the single-locus model cannot exhibit negative reciprocity at thermodynamic equilibrium but it can do so if the model is away from equilibrium.
evidence: Based on mathematical analysis of the single-locus model

claim: The single-locus model can exhibit negative reciprocity if it is away from thermodynamic equilibrium.
source: We find that the single-locus model cannot exhibit negative reciprocity at thermodynamic equilibrium but it can do so if the model is away from equilibrium.
evidence: Based on mathematical analysis of the single-locus model

claim: Sox2 and Oct4 bind at many loci in the genome with widely differing strengths and cooperativities.
source: Sox2 and Oct4 bind at many loci in the genome, with widely differing strengths and cooperativities.
evidence: Based on general knowledge about TF binding

claim: If both types of loci exhibit positive cooperativity or both exhibit negative cooperativity, then the reciprocity remains positive in the genomic-diversity model.
source: We find that if both kinds of loci exhibit positive cooperativity or both exhibit negative cooperativity, then the reciprocity remains positive.
evidence: Based on mathematical analysis of the genomic-diversity model

claim: Negative reciprocity can arise in the genomic-diversity model if the model is away from thermodynamic equilibrium.
source: However, negative reciprocity can now arise in two ways. First, if the model is away from thermodynamic equilibrium due to energy expenditure behind the scenes
evidence: Based on mathematical analysis of the genomic-diversity model

claim: Negative reciprocity can arise in the genomic-diversity model at equilibrium if loci exhibit mixed cooperativities.
source: and, second, if the model is at equilibrium but the loci exhibit mixed cooperativities, with one kind of locus being positive and the other kind being negative, so that Sox2 and Oct4 both help and hinder each other in binding across the genome.
evidence: Based on mathematical analysis of the genomic-diversity model

claim: The available data do not distinguish between energy expenditure and mixed cooperativity as explanations for negative reciprocity.
source: The available data do not distinguish between these two non-exclusive possibilities, either of which could account for the data of Chen et al.
evidence: Based on analysis of both possible explanations

claim: Evidence of mixed cooperativity across the genome or of energy expenditure has not previously been found in living cells.
source: Evidence of mixed cooperativity across the genome or of energy expenditure has not previously been found in living cells and suggests unexpected complexity 'behind the scenes' in how Sox2 and Oct4 interact on DNA.
evidence: Based on review of prior literature

claim: Single-molecule methods provide novel detection capabilities for studying TF interactions.
source: The single-molecule methods of Chen et al. offer exciting capabilities for unravelling such mechanisms.
evidence: Based on assessment of the experimental methodology

claim: The cycle condition at thermodynamic equilibrium cannot be derived from classical thermodynamics.
source: The cycle condition at thermodynamic equilibrium, also known as 'detailed balance' or 'microscopic reversibility', cannot be derived from classical thermodynamics, in which the concept of thermodynamic equilibrium was first formulated.
evidence: Based on fundamental physics knowledge

claim: The cycle condition rests on the time-reversal symmetry of the laws of physics.
source: It rests, instead, on the time-reversal symmetry of the laws of physics (Tolman, 1938; Mahan, 1975).
evidence: Supported by citations to physics literature

claim: The authors use the opposite convention to Chen et al., with the binding rate in the numerator.
source: For reasons explained below, it is better to use the opposite convention, with the binding rate in the numerator, as above in the Introduction.
evidence: Describes the authors' methodological choice

claim: The linear framework is based on graphs with directed edges that carry labels.
source: To make the underlying physics more explicit, we use the 'linear framework' developed in Gunawardena, 2012; Mirzaev and Gunawardena (2013) and recently applied to gene regulation (Ahsendorf et al., 2014; Estrada et al., 2016); for a review, see Gunawardena (2014b). One advantage of the framework is that it is based on similar pictures to that in Figure 1A, with a biochemical system being described mathematically by a graph with directed edges that carry labels (hereafter, a 'graph').
evidence: Describes the mathematical framework used, supported by citations

claim: The vertices of the graph represent the microstates of the system.
source: The vertices of the graph represent the microstates of the system, corresponding, as it were, to snapshots taken from a nanoscopic drone hovering over DNA.
evidence: Defines the mathematical representation

claim: The directed edges of the graph represent stochastic transitions between microstates.
source: The directed edges of the graph represent stochastic transitions between microstates, as would be seen in a video from our nanoscopic drone.
evidence: Defines the mathematical representation

claim: The use of concentrations is a reasonable approximation if there are many more TF molecules than binding sites.
source: The use of concentrations is a reasonable approximation if there are many more TF molecules than binding sites, which appears to be the case here (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: Justifies a modeling assumption based on experimental context

claim: The models used are highly coarse-grained with effective parameters.
source: The models used here are highly 'coarse-grained', with 'effective' parameters that are intended to summarise those molecular complexities which have not been explicitly included.
evidence: Describes the nature of the modeling approach

claim: A Markov process yields a differential equation describing how microstate probabilities change over time.
source: A Markov process yields a differential equation which describes how the probabilities for being in each microstate change over time.
evidence: Describes the mathematical properties of Markov processes

claim: The steady-state assumption is used implicitly throughout Chen et al.'s analysis.
source: The steady-state assumption is used implicitly throughout the analysis made by Chen et al.
evidence: Identifies an assumption in Chen et al.'s work

claim: At thermodynamic equilibrium, the ratio of binding label to unbinding label is determined solely by the free-energy difference between microstates.
source: There is a particularly important relationship between the free-energy minima and the edge labels at thermodynamic equilibrium: the ratio of the binding label to the unbinding label is determined solely by the free-energy difference between the corresponding microstates.
evidence: Based on fundamental statistical mechanics

claim: Equation 3 is one of the basic equations of statistical mechanics and goes back to Boltzmann and Maxwell.
source: Equation 3 is one of the basic equations of statistical mechanics and goes back to Boltzmann and Maxwell.
evidence: Historical attribution of a fundamental equation

claim: The ratio of binding to unbinding edge label is a thermodynamic quantity determined by free-energy minima.
source: Equation 3 tells us that the ratio of the binding to unbinding edge label is a thermodynamic quantity, in the sense that it is determined by just the free-energy minima.
evidence: Based on interpretation of Equation 3

claim: Individual edge labels are kinetic, not thermodynamic, quantities.
source: The individual edge labels are kinetic, not thermodynamic, quantities: they depend on the overall shape of the free-energy landscape and not just on its minima.
evidence: Based on biophysical analysis

claim: At thermodynamic equilibrium, each pair of binding and unbinding edges must be in balance independently of other edges.
source: The equilibrium cycle condition has a surprising consequence: each pair of binding and unbinding edges must be in balance, independently of any other edges in the graph (Gunawardena, 2012).
evidence: Based on mathematical analysis, supported by citation

claim: Detailed balance is the principle that forward and reverse fluxes are exactly balanced at equilibrium.
source: This is the principle of 'detailed balance', first introduced into chemistry by Gilbert Lewis (Lewis, 1925).
evidence: Historical attribution of the principle, supported by citation

claim: At thermodynamic equilibrium, the model in Figure 1B behaves as if it is four uncoupled pairs of transitions.
source: Despite being connected in a cycle, Equation 7 shows that the model in Figure 1B behaves as if it is four uncoupled pairs of transitions, which are linked only by the common probability distribution on the microstates.
evidence: Based on mathematical analysis of detailed balance

claim: The equilibrium steady-state probability of any microstate can be calculated by multiplying label ratios along any path from the empty microstate.
source: At equilibrium, a flux balance equation like Equation 7 holds for any pair of microstates that are linked by binding and unbinding edges. This yields a simple rule for calculating the equilibrium steady-state probability of any microstate. It is only necessary to take any contiguous path of binding and unbinding edges to that microstate from e and to multiply the label ratios along the path.
evidence: Describes a calculation method for equilibrium probabilities

claim: Detailed balance can be directly derived from the time-reversal symmetry of physical laws.
source: Detailed balance can be directly derived, without assuming an energy landscape, from the time-reversal symmetry of the physical laws that govern microscopic interactions (Tolman, 1938; Mahan, 1975).
evidence: Supported by citations to physics literature

claim: The hallmark of thermodynamic equilibrium is that one cannot tell whether a microscopic movie is running forwards or in reverse.
source: Indeed, the hallmark of thermodynamic equilibrium, as implied by Equation 7, is that we should not be able to tell whether the movie taken by our nanoscopic drone is running forwards or in reverse.
evidence: Based on the principle of microscopic reversibility

claim: Chen et al. used 2D single-molecule tracking to estimate the average residence time a TF remains bound to a specific binding site (~10 s).
source: Chen et al. used 2D single-molecule tracking to estimate the average residence time a TF remains bound to a specific binding site on DNA (~10 s)
evidence: Describes Chen et al.'s experimental methods and results

claim: Chen et al. used 3D multifocus microscopy to estimate the average residence time a TF spends between specific binding sites (~400 s).
source: and 3D multifocus microscopy to estimate the average residence time a TF spends between specific binding sites (~400 s).
evidence: Describes Chen et al.'s experimental methods and results

claim: Only a single TF could be measured at one time by the methods in Chen et al. (2014).
source: Only a single TF could be measured at one time by the methods in Chen et al. (2014).
evidence: Describes a limitation of Chen et al.'s experimental methods

claim: Chen et al. used a stably transformed 3T3 cell line that constitutively expressed one TF with the other TF under an inducible expression system.
source: To accommodate the other TF, Chen et al. undertook experiments in a stably transformed 3T3 cell line that constitutively expressed one TF, coupled to a fluorescent tag for single-molecule measurements, with the other TF under an inducible expression system.
evidence: Describes Chen et al.'s experimental design

claim: The 3T3 line does not normally express endogenous Sox2 or Oct4.
source: The 3T3 line does not normally express endogenous Sox2 or Oct4, enabling the recombinant proteins to be measured without background interference.
evidence: Describes a property of the cell line used

claim: Two cell lines were prepared: one in which Sox2 was measured and Oct4 was induced, and another in which Oct4 was measured and Sox2 was induced.
source: Two cell lines were prepared, one in which Sox2 was measured and Oct4 was induced and the other in which Oct4 was measured and Sox2 was induced.
evidence: Describes the experimental design

claim: When the specifically bound state of TF and DNA breaks apart, the rate is the same whether following the TF or the DNA.
source: This is correct for the unbinding labels: when the specifically bound state of TF and DNA breaks apart, the rate at which this happens is the same whether we follow the TF or follow the DNA.
evidence: Based on biophysical reasoning

claim: TF concentrations will differ depending on whether or not the TF is being induced.
source: A further difficulty arises because TF concentrations will differ depending on whether or not the TF is being induced.
evidence: Based on the experimental design

claim: Under maximal induction, not all sites of specific Oct4 binding are occupied at steady state.
source: They assumed that, under maximal induction, all sites of specific Oct4 binding were occupied at steady state. This is unlikely to be the case, as other studies of TF binding have shown (Morisaki et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on comparison with other studies, supported by citation

claim: The arrangement of κ ratios on either side of 1 is inconsistent with the single-locus model at thermodynamic equilibrium.
source: This arrangement of values on either side of 1 is inconsistent with Equation 17. (We will address the statistical significance of this estimate below.) Equation 18 cannot be accounted for by the single-locus model at thermodynamic equilibrium.
evidence: Based on mathematical analysis

claim: The data of Chen et al. suggest energy expenditure away from thermodynamic equilibrium based on the single-locus model.
source: Accordingly, it appears that the data of Chen et al. do suggest energy expenditure away from thermodynamic equilibrium.
evidence: Based on analysis of the single-locus model and the data

claim: With positive reciprocity, the TFs must influence each other's fractional binding in the same direction.
source: With positive reciprocity, the TFs must influence each other's fractional binding in the same direction.
evidence: Based on the definition of reciprocity

claim: The fractional binding of Sox2 decreases when Oct4 expression is increased.
source: Equation 18 tells us that the fractional binding of Sox2 decreases when Oct4 expression is increased
evidence: Based on analysis of the data

claim: The fractional binding of Oct4 increases when Sox2 expression is increased.
source: but the fractional binding of Oct4 increases when Sox2 expression is increased.
evidence: Based on analysis of the data

claim: Negative reciprocity can be found away from equilibrium in the single-locus model.
source: This cannot occur for the single-locus model at thermodynamic equilibrium but Figure 2E shows that this level of negative reciprocity can be found away from equilibrium.
evidence: Based on mathematical modeling shown in Figure 2E

claim: Steady-state probabilities can be calculated analytically away from equilibrium in the linear framework.
source: However, non-equilibrium steady states can still be calculated analytically in the linear framework, as we briefly explain here.
evidence: Describes a mathematical capability of the framework

claim: If the loci are independent, the steady-state fraction of sites bound by a TF can be calculated as an average over individual loci.
source: If the loci are independent then the steady-state fraction of sites bound by a TF can be calculated as an average over the individual loci, irrespective of whether or not the model is at thermodynamic equilibrium (Materials and methods).
evidence: Based on mathematical analysis

claim: In vitro measurements show mixed cooperativities between Sox2 and Oct4 on a wide range of naked DNA sequences.
source: In vitro measurements show mixed cooperativities between Sox2 and Oct4 on a wide range of naked DNA sequences (Chang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to experimental work

claim: Chen et al. concluded that Sox2 and Oct4 exhibit ordered assembly with Sox2 engaging target DNA first.
source: Chen et al. concluded in their paper that Sox2 and Oct4 exhibit ordered assembly, with 'Sox2 engaging the target DNA first, followed by assisted binding of Oct4' (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: Quotes Chen et al.'s conclusion

claim: The conclusion of ordered assembly is not justified by Chen et al.'s analysis.
source: As we have seen, this conclusion is not justified by their analysis and the question of binding order remains unresolved.
evidence: Based on the authors' reanalysis

claim: The experimental strategy of Chen et al. can be seen as a protocol for estimating the reciprocity of any two TFs.
source: The experimental strategy of Chen et al., of measuring each TF in turn while inducing the other, can now be seen as a protocol for estimating the reciprocity of any two TFs.
evidence: Based on generalization of the experimental approach

claim: It may be possible to account for endogenous TF expression by titrating the induced exogenous TF.
source: However, it may be possible to account for endogenous TF expression by titrating the induced exogenous TF rather than just maximally inducing it.
evidence: Proposes a potential experimental modification

claim: The data of Chen et al. may be accounted for if Sox2 and Oct4 sometimes help and sometimes hinder each other across the genome.
source: Far from Sox2 'assisting' Oct4, the data of Chen et al. may be accounted for, by the genomic-diversity model at thermodynamic equilibrium (Figure 3A), if Sox2 and Oct4 sometimes help and sometimes hinder each other across the genome.
evidence: Based on analysis of the genomic-diversity model

claim: The most compelling demonstration of non-equilibrium behavior would come from directly measuring the loss of detailed balance.
source: The most compelling demonstration of non-equilibrium behavior would come from directly measuring the loss of detailed balance (Battle et al., 2016): the movie taken by our nanoscopic drone should look different when played in reverse.
evidence: Proposes an experimental test, supported by citation

claim: Methods for imaging TFs at a specific genomic locus offer promise for measuring detailed balance.
source: Methods for imaging TFs at a specific genomic locus offer promise for achieving this.
evidence: Suggests a potential experimental approach

claim: The reality within a cell is not described by any model; at best, a model accurately describes our assumptions about that reality.
source: The reality within a cell is not described by any model; at best, a model accurately describes our assumptions about that reality (Gunawardena, 2014a).
evidence: Philosophical statement about models, supported by citation

claim: The single-locus model predicts that Sox2 and Oct4 action requires energy expenditure away from thermodynamic equilibrium.
source: The single-locus model (Figure 2B and C) predicts that the action of Sox2 and Oct4 requires energy expenditure away from thermodynamic equilibrium
evidence: Based on analysis of the single-locus model

claim: The genomic-diversity model offers a different explanation for the same data than the single-locus model.
source: but the genomic-diversity model (Figure 3A) offers a different explanation for the same data.
evidence: Based on analysis of the genomic-diversity model

claim: Higher order cooperativity may have a more pronounced impact than pairwise cooperativity.
source: Our results show that pairwise cooperativity does affect our conclusions, so it is plausible that higher-order cooperativity does too. Indeed, it may have a more pronounced impact (Estrada et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on inference from results and supported by citation

claim: Higher-order cooperativity appears essential and plausible on theoretical grounds.
source: At present, we know little about such higher-order effects, other than that they appear essential and plausible on theoretical grounds (Estrada et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical work

claim: The conclusions drawn from models are contingent on the underlying assumptions and may change as we learn more.
source: It is crucial to make these underlying assumptions visible and to acknowledge that the conclusions drawn are contingent upon them and may be subject to change as we learn more.
evidence: Philosophical statement about scientific modeling

claim: Experiment and theory will have to work hand in hand to figure out how biology really works.
source: We conclude that experiment and theory will have to work hand in hand if we are to figure out how biology really works (Phillips, 2015; Goldstein, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to perspectives on integrating theory and experiment
